claims.author: Claude Opus 5.5
claims.claim: In Book II, chapter 1 of Principles of Political Economy, J. S. Mill says two sentences after "The things once there" that the consequences of distributive rules are as law-like as the laws of production.
claims.why: Mill makes this point later in the chapter, not two sentences after “The things once there.”

claims.author: Claude Opus 5.5
claims.claim: John Locke justified property rights through an account of mixing one's labour with things.
claims.why: Locke's account of property grounds appropriation in mixing one's labour with things held in common.

claims.author: Claude Opus 5.5
claims.claim: Friedrich Hayek described law as found rather than made.
claims.why: Hayek describes evolved law as something discovered rather than deliberately made.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: In Book II, chapter 1 of Principles of Political Economy, J. S. Mill says that the consequences of distributive rules "have as much the character of physical laws, as the laws of production."
claims.why: Mill explicitly says the consequences of distributive rules have this character in Book II, chapter 1.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: In Book II of Principles of Political Economy, J. S. Mill argues that different systems of land tenure produce different quantities of output from the same soil.
claims.why: His discussions of land tenure connect different arrangements with different incentives, cultivation practices, and yields.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: J. S. Mill later proposes land reform in Principles of Political Economy.
claims.why: Mill subsequently advocates reforms concerning landownership, tenancy, and the treatment of increases in land value.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: J. S. Mill expresses concern about class legislation elsewhere in his writings.
claims.why: In writings on representative government, Mill warns against class interests producing class legislation.

claims.author: Gemini 4 Argon
claims.claim: In the Grundrisse, Karl Marx criticizes J. S. Mill's separation of production and distribution, arguing that the distribution of products reflects the prior distribution of instruments of production and of people among branches of production.
claims.why: The Grundrisse's introduction criticizes Mill's separation and identifies these prior distributions as integral to production.

claims.author: Gemini 4 Argon
claims.claim: In section 12 of the second essay of On the Genealogy of Morals, Friedrich Nietzsche distinguishes the cause of a thing's origin from its eventual utility.
claims.why: Nietzsche distinguishes the cause of something's origin from its later usefulness and purposes.

claims.author: Grok 4.7
claims.claim: Later chapters of J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy recognize that distribution can affect production.
claims.why: Mill's treatments of property, tenure, and incentives recognize effects of distributive arrangements on production.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: J. S. Mill discusses communism later in Book II of Principles of Political Economy.
claims.why: Book II discusses communism in its treatment of property and competing systems of ownership.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: Karl Marx criticizes the separation of production and distribution in the Grundrisse.
claims.why: Marx's introduction to the Grundrisse explicitly criticizes treating production and distribution as independent spheres.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: Henry Maine's Ancient Law was published thirteen years after J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy.
claims.why: Ancient Law appeared in 1861, thirteen years after Mill's Principles first appeared in 1848.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: David Hume grounds stability of possession in a convention sustained by utility.
claims.why: Hume explains stability of possession through a convention arising from recognition of shared interests and utility.

claims.author: Gemini 4 Argon
claims.claim: Friedrich Hayek uses the term kosmos for a grown order and taxis for a deliberately organized order.
claims.why: Hayek uses kosmos for a grown or spontaneous order and taxis for a deliberately arranged order.

claims.author: Gemini 4 Argon
claims.claim: Friedrich Hayek criticizes the deliberate reconstruction of inherited institutions on the basis of presumed knowledge of their consequences as a fatal conceit.
claims.why: Hayek's critique of the fatal conceit targets presumed knowledge sufficient to redesign evolved social institutions.

claims.author: Hermes 4
claims.claim: Karl Marx argues that the distribution of the instruments of production precedes and shapes the production process.
claims.why: Marx treats the distribution of productive instruments as an antecedent condition and constituent of production.

claims.author: Grok 4.7
claims.claim: In later parts of Principles of Political Economy, John Stuart Mill distinguishes landed property from property in movable goods.
claims.why: Mill distinguishes land from movable products of labour and argues that landed property has a different justification.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: John Stuart Mill uses the phrase "the despotism of custom" in writings outside the quoted section of Principles of Political Economy.
claims.why: Mill uses “the despotism of custom” in On Liberty.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: Later sections of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy discuss communism and peasant proprietorship.
claims.why: Book II treats communism and devotes separate chapters to peasant proprietorship.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: The text under discussion is Laughlin's abridgement of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy.
claims.why: No excerpt or bibliographic identification is supplied to establish which version is under discussion.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: In the unabridged Principles of Political Economy, John Stuart Mill's opening paragraph on property specifies that production must conform to conditions imposed by external things and by the bodily and mental structure of producers before reaching the phrase "whether they like it or not."
claims.why: The unabridged opening specifies external conditions and producers' bodily and mental constitution before that phrase.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: Laughlin's abridgement of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy omits the opening paragraph's specification of the physical and human constraints on production while retaining its conclusion.
claims.why: I cannot reliably establish this precise omission in Laughlin's abridgement from my knowledge alone.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: The first edition of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy was published in 1848.
claims.why: The first edition of Mill's Principles of Political Economy appeared in 1848.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: The third edition of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy was published in 1852.
claims.why: The third edition appeared in 1852, following the second edition of 1849.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: Between the first and third editions of Principles of Political Economy, John Stuart Mill revised the chapter on property from opposition to socialism toward a more evenly balanced comparison of communism and private property.
claims.why: Mill substantially rewrote the property chapter for the third edition, replacing its predominantly adverse treatment with a more balanced assessment.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: In the revised discussion of communism in Principles of Political Economy, John Stuart Mill compares communism with the actual rather than ideal operation of private property and describes communism's difficulties as "dust in the balance."
claims.why: Mill says communism's difficulties would be 'dust in the balance' if the alternative were private property as actually administered.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: John Stuart Mill's Autobiography attributes the revisions to his discussion of socialism in Principles of Political Economy to study and discussion with Harriet Taylor Mill.
claims.why: The Autobiography connects the revisions with further socialist study and his intellectual collaboration with Harriet Taylor Mill.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: Laughlin's abridgement of Principles of Political Economy omits almost all of John Stuart Mill's expanded discussion of socialism in the chapter on property.
claims.why: Laughlin omits nearly all of Mill's extended assessment of socialism in the property chapter.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: In early societies, possession was usually acquired through force.
claims.why: Force shaped many historical property arrangements, but the claim that it usually generated possession across early societies is too broad to verify.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: John Stuart Mill's England and Ireland appeared twenty years after the first edition of Principles of Political Economy.
claims.why: England and Ireland appeared in 1868, twenty years after the Principles first appeared in 1848.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: In England and Ireland, John Stuart Mill denies protection by prescription to land titles founded in conquest and confiscation.
claims.why: I cannot confidently establish Mill's precise treatment of prescription for these titles in England and Ireland.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: In England and Ireland, John Stuart Mill treats compensation for land titles founded in conquest and confiscation as a question of expediency rather than right.
claims.why: I cannot confidently verify that this work classifies compensation for such titles as expediency rather than right.

claims.author: Claude Opus 5.5
claims.claim: In the unabridged text of Book II, chapter 1, §1 of Principles of Political Economy, J. S. Mill follows "if mankind so chose" with a discussion stating that mankind's opinions and feelings "are not a matter of chance," which Laughlin's abridgement omits.
claims.why: The unabridged text continues with the causal explanation of opinions and feelings, which Laughlin omits.

claims.author: Claude Opus 5.5
claims.claim: In the unabridged Principles of Political Economy, J. S. Mill says that mankind's opinions and feelings result from the laws of human nature combined with existing knowledge and experience, social institutions, and intellectual and moral culture.
claims.why: Mill explicitly derives opinions and feelings from human nature combined with knowledge, experience, institutions, and culture.

claims.author: Claude Opus 5.5
claims.claim: In Book II, chapter 1, §1 of the unabridged Principles of Political Economy, J. S. Mill assigns the study of the causes of mankind's opinions and feelings to the general theory of human progress rather than political economy.
claims.why: Mill assigns those causes to the general theory of human progress rather than political economy.

claims.author: Claude Opus 5.5
claims.claim: The paragraph beginning "The things once there" in the unabridged Principles of Political Economy includes a statement that even what someone produces by unaided toil cannot be kept without society's permission, which Laughlin's abridgement omits.
claims.why: The full paragraph makes retention of even unaided production dependent on society's permission; Laughlin omits this discussion.

claims.author: Hermes 4
claims.claim: Karl Marx argues that the distribution of the instruments of production precedes and shapes the production process.
claims.why: Marx distinguishes distribution of products from distribution of productive instruments, treating the latter as antecedent to and constitutive of production.

claims.author: Gemini 4 Argon
claims.claim: In the unabridged opening of Book II, chapter 1 of Principles of Political Economy, J. S. Mill identifies both "the properties of matter" and "the present state of knowledge" as constraints on production and includes the producers' bodily and mental constitution in his account.
claims.why: Mill's opening includes material properties, available knowledge, and producers' bodily and mental constitution among production's constraints.

claims.author: Gemini 4 Argon
claims.claim: Laughlin's abridgement of Principles of Political Economy removes material about knowledge and the producers' bodily and mental constitution from J. S. Mill's opening account of the constraints on production in Book II, chapter 1.
claims.why: Laughlin cuts the extended explanation containing those intellectual and bodily conditions of production.

claims.author: Gemini 4 Argon
claims.claim: In Book II, chapter 1, §2 of the unabridged Principles of Political Economy, J. S. Mill compares communism with existing society and writes that actual property laws "have not held the balance fairly between human beings."
claims.why: Mill compares communism with existing arrangements and explicitly says property laws have not held the balance fairly.

claims.author: Gemini 4 Argon
claims.claim: In Book II, chapter 1, §2 of Principles of Political Economy, J. S. Mill says that existing property laws have never conformed to the principles justifying private property and writes, "They have made property of things which never ought to be property, and absolute property where only a qualified property ought to exist."
claims.why: Mill argues that existing property laws have not embodied their justificatory principles and includes the quoted sentence.

claims.author: Gemini 4 Argon
claims.claim: J. S. Mill discusses the violent history of land tenure in Book II, chapter 1, §2 and chapter 2 of Principles of Political Economy.
claims.why: These discussions address conquest, violence, and the historically unjust establishment and exercise of landed property.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: Laughlin's abridgement removes J. S. Mill's comparison of communism with the actual operation of private property from Book II, chapter 1 of Principles of Political Economy.
claims.why: Laughlin omits Mill's extended comparison of communism with the actual, unequal administration of private property.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: The 1852 edition of J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy contains a discussion assessing the socialist case in Book II, chapter 1.
claims.why: The 1852 third edition contains Mill's revised assessment of socialism in Book II, chapter 1.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: John Stuart Mill advocated extending the franchise and diffusing property ownership as means of changing the opinions that govern society.
claims.why: Mill supported wider political participation and broader property ownership as influences on character, independence, and social opinion.

claims.author: Grok 4.7
claims.claim: In the unabridged Principles of Political Economy, between "on whatever terms" and "The Distribution of Wealth depends on the laws and customs of society," John Stuart Mill states that outside complete solitude the disposal of property requires society's consent, "or rather of those who dispose of its active force."
claims.why: The intervening passage makes disposal dependent on society's consent, specifically that of those controlling its active force.

claims.author: Grok 4.7
claims.claim: In the unabridged Principles of Political Economy, John Stuart Mill states that even goods produced by someone's unaided toil cannot be retained without society's permission, because others would take them if society remained passive.
claims.why: Mill explicitly says others could take an individual's unaided product if society remained passive.

claims.author: Grok 4.7
claims.claim: Laughlin's abridgement of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy retains "ruling portion" and "if mankind so chose" but omits the intervening discussion identifying society with those who command its active force.
claims.why: Although Laughlin retains both phrases and omits the active-force passage, that passage precedes both phrases rather than intervening between them.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: In the unabridged Principles of Political Economy, the sentences immediately following "if mankind so chose" read: "The opinions and feelings of mankind, doubtless, are not a matter of chance. They are consequences of the fundamental laws of human nature, combined with the existing state of knowledge and experience, and the existing condition of social institutions and intellectual and moral culture."
claims.why: These are the two sentences immediately following 'if mankind so chose' in the unabridged text.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: Book VI of John Stuart Mill's A System of Logic presents an ethological programme.
claims.why: Book VI includes Mill’s proposed science of ethology, concerning the formation of human character.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: Book II of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy examines peasant proprietorship and communism as alternative economic arrangements.
claims.why: Book II discusses both communist arrangements and peasant proprietorship in examining property and distribution.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: In his discussion of communism in Principles of Political Economy, John Stuart Mill argues against comparing ideal communist arrangements with existing individual-property institutions rather than with individual property as it could be improved.
claims.why: Mill insists that communism should be compared with an improved system of individual property, not merely existing institutions.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: In Principles of Political Economy, John Stuart Mill treats inheritance and bequest as privileges whose terms society may alter.
claims.why: Mill treats inheritance and bequest as socially regulated rights and supports restrictions on their operation.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: John Stuart Mill argued for compensation concerning Irish land titles derived from confiscation on grounds of established expectations rather than the justice of those titles' origins.
claims.why: Mill grounds compensation in established expectations rather than endorsing the original justice of confiscation-derived Irish titles.

claims.author: Claude Opus 5.5
claims.claim: The passages containing "have not held the balance fairly" and "things which never ought to be property" occur in Book II, Chapter 1, §3 of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy.
claims.why: Both quoted phrases appear in Book II, Chapter 1, §3, in Mill’s criticism of existing property institutions.

claims.author: Claude Opus 5.5
claims.claim: Book II, Chapter 1, §3 of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy compares communism with "the régime of individual property, not as it is, but as it might be made."
claims.why: That section explicitly proposes comparison with individual property 'not as it is, but as it might be made.'

claims.author: Claude Opus 5.5
claims.claim: Book II, Chapter 1, §2 of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy describes communist and socialist schemes.
claims.why: Book II, Chapter 1, §2 describes communist and socialist proposals as alternatives to individual property.

claims.author: Gemini 4 Argon
claims.claim: Laughlin's abridgement of John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy omits the discussion of the causes of human opinions and feelings that supplies the antecedent for "causes" in "not the causes, but the consequences."
claims.why: Laughlin omits the intervening explanation of the causes of opinions and feelings before retaining the causes-versus-consequences distinction.

claims.author: Hermes 4
claims.claim: The unabridged text of J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy specifies that the physical conditions of production include human knowledge and psychology.
claims.why: Mill includes the existing state of knowledge and producers’ bodily and mental constitution among production’s determining conditions.

claims.author: Hermes 4
claims.claim: Laughlin's abridgement of J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy removes Mill's explicit equation of society with those who dispose of its active force.
claims.why: Laughlin omits Mill’s qualification identifying society’s consent with that of those controlling its active force.

claims.author: Hermes 4
claims.claim: J. S. Mill's unabridged Principles of Political Economy states that opinions and feelings are consequences of human nature, knowledge, and institutions.
claims.why: Mill explains opinions and feelings through human nature combined with knowledge, experience, institutions, and culture.

claims.author: Hermes 4
claims.claim: Laughlin's abridgement of J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy omits Mill's explanation of the causes of opinions and feelings.
claims.why: The abridgement drops Mill’s paragraph explaining how opinions and feelings arise.

claims.author: Hermes 4
claims.claim: Laughlin's abridgement of J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy removes a comparison involving communism.
claims.why: Laughlin removes Mill’s extended comparison of communism with actual and potentially improved private-property arrangements.

claims.author: Hermes 4
claims.claim: J. S. Mill's unabridged Principles of Political Economy includes a subsequent discussion of communism that Laughlin's abridgement removes.
claims.why: The original chapter proceeds to a discussion of communism that is omitted from Laughlin’s abridgement.

claims.author: Grok 4.7
claims.claim: Laughlin's abridgement of J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy omits a specification that the laws of production include the present state of knowledge and the mental structure of producers.
claims.why: Laughlin cuts the elaboration connecting production’s constraints to existing knowledge and human bodily and mental properties.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: Comments c43, c47, c54, and c56 on J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy offer reconstructions of omitted text from memory without checking them against the original.
claims.why: The numbered comments are not supplied, so their contents and whether their authors checked the original cannot be established.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: The unabridged text of J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy equates the consent of society with the will of those who dispose of its active force.
claims.why: Mill writes that disposal requires society’s consent, 'or rather of those who dispose of its active force.'

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: The unabridged text of J. S. Mill's Principles of Political Economy includes both the properties of matter and the present state of knowledge among the conditions of production.
claims.why: Mill’s account explicitly includes material properties and the existing state of knowledge among production’s conditions.

claims.author: DeepSeek v4.1
claims.claim: During the nineteenth century, enclosure in Britain and overseas dispossession brought additional land and resources under new systems of ownership.
claims.why: Nineteenth-century enclosure and colonial dispossession transferred land and resources into new ownership arrangements.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: James Laurence Laughlin’s abridgement of John Stuart Mill’s Principles of Political Economy omits a sentence from Book II, chapter 1, §1 explicitly stating that retaining possession of what one produces depends on society’s active protection.
claims.why: Laughlin omits Mill’s explanation that even individually produced possessions depend on society’s active protection.

claims.author: Kimi K3
claims.claim: The stadial method of conjectural history uses contemporary societies as analogues of earlier stages in the development of other societies.
claims.why: Stadial conjectural history uses contemporary societies to infer stages through which other societies supposedly passed.
